Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
"There will always be the pain and the hurt now. That is never going to go away." June Steenkamp, talks to Carte Blanche, about how much it still hurts, 21 months after Reeva's passing.

Summary:
"As long as we live, as long as we breathe, Barry and I will struggle to come to terms with Reeva's death. We are locked forever in unbearable grief."

They wanted the truth of what happened that night between Reeva and Oscar and June thought that was what she was going to get by attending the his trial. But she still seeks the truth. She didn't believe Oscar. She didn't enjoy attending the trial, but felt she had to do it for Reeva. She said it was important for Oscar to know that she was there. She felt she was on "show", outside and inside the court room. "Whatever the outcome of the case, ther would always remain a void."

Further information:
Her book, published just more than two weeks after Oscar Pistorius was sentenced to five years imprisonment for the killing of her daughter, is an insight into the life of Reeva, the "glue" that held their family and June and Barry's marriage together. It is a book about a mother who had lost a child, not knowing how she will live without her for the rest of her days. June wears Reeva's clothes, jewelry and perfume, to feel closer to her. She sleeps on her linen. She believes Reeva leaves her feathers to show her she is present.

"I'm not sure we'll ever have closure."

June describes hearing that her daughter had died, never even heard of the "blade runner". She said she didn't know who Oscar Pistorius was, didn't know that he was world famous and ran in the Olympics - the first disabled athlete to compete against able-bodied athletes on that level. She didn't know what he looked like. It was only after Reeva's death that she'd seen his picture in the newspapers and heard of the blade-runner.

She doesn't want Oscar to suffer in prison, but he must serve his time. She is not sure whether they will ever get closure.
They are going to set up the Reeva Rebecca Steenkamp Foundation with shelters to help and empower other women.

Press Release:


June Steenkamp breaks her silence
The mother the whole world has prayed for and sympathised with... hers is a voice that all have waited to hear. Reeva Steenkamp’s mother June takes Carte Blanche into her home and, after almost two years of media silence, shares her most intimate thoughts about life without Reeva and more.


Script:


JUNE STEENKAMP SCRIPT
PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK

“Our lives seem to have crumbled like a sandcastle knocked by a freak wave on the beach.
“Reeva, who was simply our child, is dead. She’s gone and never coming back.”

DEVI LINK: In her book, Reeva: A mother’s story, June Steenkamp writes: “As long as we live, as long as we breathe, Barry and I will struggle to come to terms with Reeva’s death. We are locked in unbearable grief forever.”
I’m here at Summerstrand Beach in Port Elizabeth, where, on the 20th of May last year, June, her husband Barry, their family and friends scattered Reeva’s ashes .

Treasuring a single pebble picked up on the beach on that day, June and Barry now try to hold onto their memories of Reeva to try and find solace from the questions that still linger – “How can Reeva be dead? What had been going on in her life that she could end up in such a situation with such a man?”
Barry and June are struggling to come to terms with the passing of Reeva, the only child they had together. She was their “whole life, the backbone and glue of their family”.

JUNE STEENKAMP [FEBRUARY 2013] I had a phone call at half past seven in the morning, that morning, they said there’s been an accident and she’s been shot and I said, all I want to know now is if she is alive or if she’s dead and then the man said, he was with the police, and he said, I’m sorry to have to tell you but I don’t want you to go out and read it in the paper but she is dead.

Since then, having endured a court case that lasted eight months and with Oscar Pistorius sent to prison for five years, they’ve been re-living what they call “their nightmare – the vision of Reeva suffering this terrible trauma. Her terror and helplessness”. June has written a book - a dedication, she says, to her daughter. It’s about Reeva’s life, what she knew of her daughter’s relationship with Oscar and what June has had to live through since Reeva’s death.

DEVI: What has it been like for you?

JUNE: It is the most terrible thing that could happen to anyone, I wouldn’t wish it upon anyone. It’s just too ... you can’t explain in words, it is like a pain in your heart and deep in your soul. It’s about her – the loss and her suffering.

DEVI: Is it getting better?

JUNE: It can never get better, unless someone can bring her back to life, it’s never going to better. You’ve got to learn to live with it so you can get on with your life. The poem, God’s Child, “If I give you a child, will you care for that child? I’m sending her to earth because there are things on the earth that I want her to learn but don’t be upset when I come to fetch her again,” because I can understand now that she was a gift from God. And I just had her for a short time.

DEVI: Has that helped you to find some sort of closure?

JUNE: It’s not closure; we are never going to get closure. I think you are crazy if you ever think you are going to get closure in this kind of a situation, you can’t.

DEVI: What do you miss most about Reeva?

JUNE: Her attention, I miss most of all her attention and just that I can’t pick up the phone and speak to her, you know, that’s hard, that’s hard and all of her clothes – this is her jacket – I love the things that – every single day when I’m choosing a jacket, I choose this jacket. It’s becoming my uniform, it just brings her closer to me.

DEVI: You sleep on her linen, you wear her rings?

JUNE: Ja…

DEVI: What was your relationship like with Reeva?

JUNE: It was so close. We had that pact that if one of us died, we would let the other know, you know, we would send each other messages.

June believes Reeva is sending her messages by leaving feathers in her path. They are a sign to June that Reeva is okay.

JUNE: Just after she died there were the feathers, always the feathers. As I was leaving to go to court, there was one outside the B&B where we stayed and they were in places where the windows weren’t open so they couldn’t blow, it was just amazing and I picked that up as being her message to me that she is fine where she is.

DEVI: How did you find out that Oscar and Reeva were a couple, an item, that they were seeing each other?

JUNE: I didn’t know him as a person, I’d never heard of him and the first time I saw them together was on the red carpet at the Sport’s Awards. I asked her and she said he was just a friend.

DEVI: So it wasn’t a big deal for you?

JUNE: No, I mean we didn’t know of any relationship going on with him.

DEVI: You say in the book that you lost touch with Reeva for about three months.

JUNE: I did.
DEVI: What happened?

JUNE: I don’t know – he happened.

In her book June says she kept on trying to work out how, or why Reeva decided to be with Oscar and thinks that ultimately she felt sorry for him. Of Reeva, she says: “She was a nurturer, a carer, she wanted to look after him.”

JUNE: I don’t get this, I don’t get why she followed ... she took the wrong turn, she took a wrong turning.

DEVI: Do you believe Oscar’s version of events?

JUNE: No.

DEVI: Not even for a minute?

JUNE: No.

DEVI: You don’t think that it could be plausible?

JUNE: I’ve never even thought or considered that. I’ve never considered that, because I don’t believe in my heart that it is true.

DEVI: At the time of the trial, Barry said the trial would bring out the truth. Do you think that happened?

JUNE: No, most definitely not.

DEVI: What do you think happened?

JUNE: I think they had an argument and he lost his temper.

DEVI: What was it like that first day when you saw him in court?

JUNE: I don’t know, it’s hard to describe where you know him being there in front of me. He had to actually walk right past me every day and when I first saw him I thought: ‘this is the person that’s killed my daughter’ and I think that I, in a way, unnerved him and I liked that part of it.

DEVI: Why?

JUNE: I don’t know. I wanted to be there for Reeva so to me it was good that I unnerved him.

DEVI: And when he was retching and crying? You were right there? You could hear him?



JUNE: Yes, yes but you’ve got to realise something. He was not crying for Reeva. He was crying for himself.

DEVI: Reeva became the deceased ...

JUNE: She became invisible.

DEVI: She became Oscar Pistorius’s girlfriend.

JUNE: Yes. It made me so happy that Carte Blanche had kept her alive with those beautiful things. When we saw those it was uplifting to us too, you know, that somebody was rooting for her.

While June was in Pretoria attending the trial, Barry watched it at home. He suffered a stroke two months after Reeva died and was still recovering. He only attended the verdict and sentencing.
In PE, he tries to find peace and answers in the stillness of being with the horses he trains. The tragedy broke him… and for a long time, he couldn’t even say Reeva’s name. He didn’t want to be interviewed.

DEVI: How is Barry coping?

JUNE: He’s a lot better. He is not as emotional, he can get through things now, he’s a lot better.

DEVI: Do you think Judge Masipa made a mistake?

JUNE: I don’t want to say that, because she has to judge on what was before her. She had that. That is what she had to work with.

DEVI: You wanted to take the witness stand, why?

JUNE: I just was possessed with wanting to say things, but I was advised not to do it and I wouldn’t have gotten through it. I maybe would have said two words and then I would have been a mess.

DEVI: You’ve heard the criticism, the criticism that you were using Reeva’s death and her name for commercial gain?

JUNE: Yes, exactly.

DEVI: That you financially gained from talking to international media because they would pay. Set the record straight.

JUNE: You don’t get paid by newspapers, they don’t pay you. We did HELLO! magazine, we did YOU magazine and Huisgenoot. People must realise that when this happened we were bankrupt, we had nothing. We didn’t even have food on the table. These people who are, who say these things, it is none of their business first of all and secondly, they’ve never walked in our shoes. Let their daughter be brutally murdered and see how they get on with it.

During the trial, it was revealed that Oscar had, since March last year, been paying the Steenkamps an amount of R6000 a month. According to June, the Pistorius’s approached them and asked that the deal be kept confidential. It was placed on the court record that June and Barry were later in a position to pay Oscar back.

DEVI: Why did you and Barry say yes to it?

JUNE: I’m not saying we were comfortable with it. It’s because we were destitute. That money was supposed to come out of a civil case, it was supposed to be a loan to us from the civil case and there were other offers made to us from Oscar and then eventually I decided, well Barry and I decided, we don’t want his money, it’s like blood money, we don’t want it.

DEVI: What did it feel like taking that money every single month?

JUNE: It wasn’t pleasant, but it was an agreement and they asked to keep it quiet and then they brought it out when it suited them.

DEVI: How do you feel about Oscar now?

JUNE: I don’t feel anything, he’s nothing to me. I feel angry for what he’s done to her. It’s my child, I gave birth to her.

DEVI: What was going through your mind when Oscar apologised to you and Barry?

JUNE: It didn’t mean a thing to me. They were words. “Sorry,” can never cover what he’d done. He wanted to see us, he did try and make an appointment, but we weren’t ready to face him.

DEVI: Do you think you’ll ever be ready to face him?

JUNE: I think so. I think I’d like to look in his face and he can see exactly what he’s done to us and what he has taken away from us.

DEVI: What would you say to him?

JUNE: I would say: “Here, I’m the mother and you’ve taken everything out of our life.”

DEVI: Do you think Oscar gets that?

JUNE: I don’t think so.

DEVI: Do you think you will ever know the truth, that you will find out ...

JUNE: Well, we are still hoping that the truth will somehow come out. I’m sure he remembers when he carried her down those stairs. He will remember that for the rest of his life.

DEVI: Have you forgiven him?

JUNE: I have forgiven him. If you are a Christian, you have to forgive otherwise you are going to carry all this pain inside you, this hatred and I don’t want to, I’m not like that.

DEVI: Do you ever cry?

JUNE: Yes, when she did her farewell on Tropika and she said good bye, she - *shows kissing with fingers* - that was for me, that was for me. And when I read, I’m going to cry now, when I read that poem, I cried all the way through that poem, because to me, that is what she was for me: a child from God.

DEVI: You come across as being constantly strong and ...

JUNE: No, but the feelings are strong too, the hurt and missing her is very strong.

She cannot bring Reeva back, but the feathers she receives gives her strength to carry on.

DEVI: You wanted to take the witness stand, why? JUNE: I just was possessed with wanting to say things, but I was advised not to do it and I wouldn’t have gotten through it. I maybe would have said two words and then I would have been a mess. DEVI: You’ve heard the criticism, the criticism that you were using Reeva’s death and her name for commercial gain? JUNE: Yes, exactly. DEVI: That you financially gained from talking to international media because they would pay. Set the record straight. JUNE: You don’t get paid by newspapers, they don’t pay you. We did HELLO! magazine, we did YOU magazine and Huisgenoot. People must realise that when this happened we were bankrupt, we had nothing. We didn’t even have food on the table. These people who are, who say these things, it is none of their business first of all and secondly, they’ve never walked in our shoes. Let their daughter be brutally murdered and see how they get on with it. During the trial, it was revealed that Oscar had, since March last year, been paying the Steenkamps an amount of R6000 a month. According to June, the Pistorius’s approached them and asked that the deal be kept confidential. It was placed on the court record that June and Barry were later in a position to pay Oscar back. DEVI: Why did you and Barry say yes to it? JUNE: I’m not saying we were comfortable with it. It’s because we were destitute. That money was supposed to come out of a civil case, it was supposed to be a loan to us from the civil case and there were other offers made to us from Oscar and then eventually I decided, well Barry and I decided, we don’t want his money, it’s like blood money, we don’t want it. DEVI: What did it feel like taking that money every single month? JUNE: It wasn’t pleasant, but it was an agreement and they asked to keep it quiet and then they brought it out when it suited them. DEVI: How do you feel about Oscar now? JUNE: I don’t feel anything, he’s nothing to me. I feel angry for what he’s done to her. It’s my child, I gave birth to her. DEVI: What was going through your mind when Oscar apologised to you and Barry? JUNE: It didn’t mean a thing to me. They were words. “Sorry,” can never cover what he’d done. He wanted to see us, he did try and make an appointment, but we weren’t ready to face him. DEVI: Do you think you’ll ever be ready to face him? JUNE: I think so. I think I’d like to look in his face and he can see exactly what he’s done to us and what he has taken away from us. DEVI: What would you say to him? JUNE: I would say: “Here, I’m the mother and you’ve taken everything out of our life.” DEVI: Do you think Oscar gets that? JUNE: I don’t think so. DEVI: Do you think you will ever know the truth, that you will find out ... JUNE: Well, we are still hoping that the truth will somehow come out. I’m sure he remembers when he carried her down those stairs. He will remember that for the rest of his life. DEVI: Have you forgiven him? JUNE: I have forgiven him. If you are a Christian, you have to forgive otherwise you are going to carry all this pain inside you, this hatred and I don’t want to, I’m not like that. DEVI: Do you ever cry? JUNE: Yes, when she did her farewell on Tropika and she said good bye, she - *shows kissing with fingers* - that was for me, that was for me. And when I read, I’m going to cry now, when I read that poem, I cried all the way through that poem, because to me, that is what she was for me: a child from God. DEVI: You come across as being constantly strong and ... JUNE: No, but the feelings are strong too, the hurt and missing her is very strong. She cannot bring Reeva back, but the feathers she receives gives her strength to carry on. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): "There will always be the pain and the hurt now. That is never going to go away." June Steenkamp, talks to Carte Blanche, about how much it still hurts, 21 months after Reeva's passing.
metadata.Summary: "As long as we live, as long as we breathe, Barry and I will struggle to come to terms with Reeva's death. We are locked forever in unbearable grief." They wanted the truth of what happened that night between Reeva and Oscar and June thought that was what she was going to get by attending the his trial. But she still seeks the truth. She didn't believe Oscar. She didn't enjoy attending the trial, but felt she had to do it for Reeva. She said it was important for Oscar to know that she was there. She felt she was on "show", outside and inside the court room. "Whatever the outcome of the case, ther would always remain a void."
metadata.Further information: Her book, published just more than two weeks after Oscar Pistorius was sentenced to five years imprisonment for the killing of her daughter, is an insight into the life of Reeva, the "glue" that held their family and June and Barry's marriage together. It is a book about a mother who had lost a child, not knowing how she will live without her for the rest of her days. June wears Reeva's clothes, jewelry and perfume, to feel closer to her. She sleeps on her linen. She believes Reeva leaves her feathers to show her she is present. "I'm not sure we'll ever have closure." June describes hearing that her daughter had died, never even heard of the "blade runner". She said she didn't know who Oscar Pistorius was, didn't know that he was world famous and ran in the Olympics - the first disabled athlete to compete against able-bodied athletes on that level. She didn't know what he looked like. It was only after Reeva's death that she'd seen his picture in the newspapers and heard of the blade-runner. She doesn't want Oscar to suffer in prison, but he must serve his time. She is not sure whether they will ever get closure. They are going to set up the Reeva Rebecca Steenkamp Foundation with shelters to help and empower other women.
